source_text: 9.6 Πίστεώς ἐστιν ἀπόδειξις τὰ θηρία. Πέποιθας ἐπὶ Κύριον; Ἐπὶ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ, καὶ καταπατήσεις λέοντα καὶ δράκοντα. Καὶ ἔχεις τὴν διὰ πίστεως ἐξουσίαν πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων. Ἢ οὐχ ὁρᾷς ὅτι φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ ἐνάψας ὁ ἔχις οὐδεμίαν προσετρίψατο βλάβην, διὰ τὸ πλήρη πίστεως εὑρεθῆναι τὸν ἅγιον; Εἰ δὲ ἄπιστος εἶ, φοβοῦ μὴ μᾶλλον τὸ θηρίον ἢ τὴν σεαυτοῦ ἀπιστίαν, δι' ἧς πάσῃ φθορᾷ σεαυτὸν εὐάλωτον κατεσκεύασας. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ αἰσθάνομαι πάλαι τὰ περὶ τῆς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου γενέσεως ἀπαιτούμενος, καὶ μονονουχὶ ἀκούειν δοκῶ μοι τῶν ἀκροατῶν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις καταβοώντων, ὅτι τὰ μὲν ἡμέτερα ὁποῖά τινά ἐστι τὴν φύσιν διδασκόμεθα, ἡμᾶς δὲ αὐτοὺς ἀγνοοῦμεν. Ἀνάγκη οὖν εἰπεῖν, τὸν κατέχοντα ἡμᾶς ὄκνον παρωσαμένους. Τῷ ὄντι γὰρ ἔοικε πάντων εἶναι χαλεπώτατον ἑαυτὸν ἐπιγνῶναι. Οὐ γὰρ μόνον ὀφθαλμὸς τὰ ἔξω βλέπων ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν οὐ κέχρηται τῷ ὁρᾶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς ἡμῶν ὁ νοῦς, ὀξέως τὸ ἀλλότριον ἁμάρτημα καταβλέπων, βραδύς ἐστι πρὸς τὴν τῶν οἰκείων ἐλαττωμάτων ἐπίγνωσιν. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ νῦν ὁ λόγος, ὀξέως ἐπελθὼν τὰ ἀλλότρια, νωθρός ἐστι καὶ ὄκνου πλήρης πρὸς τὴν τῶν οἰκείων ἐξέτασιν· καίτοι οὐ μᾶλλον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς τὸν Θεὸν ἔστιν ἐπιγνῶναι, ἢ καὶ ἐκ τῆς οἰκείας ἡμῶν κατασκευῆς, τόν γε συνετῶς ἑαυτὸν ἐξετάσαντα· ὥς φησιν ὁ προφήτης· Ἐθαυμαστώθη ἡ γνῶσίς σου ἐξ ἐμοῦ· τουτέστιν, ἐμαυτὸν καταμαθὼν, τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τῆς ἐν σοὶ σοφίας ἐξεδιδάχθην. Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον. Ποῦ μοι ὁ Ἰουδαῖος, ὃς, ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν, ὥσπερ διὰ θυρίδων τινῶν, τοῦ τῆς θεολογίας φωτὸς διαλάμποντος, καὶ δευτέρου προσώπου τοῦ ὑποδεικνυμένου μὲν μυστικῶς, οὔπω δὲ ἐναργῶς ἐκφανέντος, πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀπεμάχετο, αὐτὸν ἑαυτῷ λέγων τὸν Θεὸν διαλέγεσθαι; Αὐτὸς γὰρ εἶπε, φησὶ, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐποίησε. Γενηθήτω φῶς, καὶ ἐγένετο φῶς. Ἦν μὲν οὖν καὶ τότε πρόχειρος ἐν τοῖς παρ' αὐτῶν λεγομένοις ἡ ἀτοπία. Τίς γὰρ χαλκεὺς, ἢ τέκτων, ἢ σκυτοτόμος, ἐπὶ τῶν ὀργάνων τῆς τέχνης μόνος καθήμενος, οὐδενὸς αὐτῷ συνεργοῦντος, λέγει αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ, ποιήσωμεν τὴν μάχαιραν, ἢ συμπήξωμεν τὸ ἄροτρον, ἢ ἀπεργασώμεθα τὸ ὑπόδημα· ἀλλ' οὐχὶ σιωπῇ τὴν ἐπιβάλλουσαν ἐνέργειαν ἐκτελεῖ; Φλυαρία γὰρ τῷ ὄντι δεινὴ, ἄρχοντά τινα ἑαυτοῦ καὶ ἐπιστάτην καθῆσθαι, δεσποτικῶς ἑαυτοῦ καὶ σφοδρῶς κατασπεύδοντα. Ἀλλ' ὅμως οἱ αὐτὸν τὸν Κύριον συκοφαντῆσαι μὴ κατοκνήσαντες, τί οὐκ ἂν εἴποιεν γεγυμνασμένην πρὸς τὸ ψεῦδος τὴν γλῶσσαν ἔχοντες; Ἡ μέντοι παροῦσα φωνὴ παντελῶς αὐτῶν ἀποφράσσει τὸ στόμα. Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον. Μὴ καὶ νῦν, εἰπέ μοι, μεμονωμένον ἐστὶ τὸ πρόσωπον; Οὐ γὰρ γέγραπται, γενηθήτω ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλὰ, Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον. Ἕως οὔπω ὁ διδασκόμενος παρεφαίνετο, ἐν βάθει ἐκεκάλυπτο τῆς θεολογίας τὸ κήρυγμα· ὅτε λοιπὸν ἀνθρώπου γένεσις προσδοκᾶται, παραγυμνοῦται ἡ πίστις, καὶ τρανότερον παραδηλοῦται τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ δόγμα. Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον. Ἀκούεις, ὦ χριστομάχε, ὅτι τῷ κοινωνῷ τῆς δημιουργίας προσδιαλέγεται, δι' οὗ καὶ τοὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησεν, ὃς φέρει τὰ σύμπαντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ. Ἀλλ' οὐ γὰρ ἡσυχῇ παραδέχεται τὸν λόγον τῆς εὐσεβείας· ὥσπερ δὲ τῶν θηρίων τὰ μισανθρωπότατα, ἐπειδὰν τοῖς ζώγροις ἐναποκλεισθῇ, περιβρύχεται τοῖς κυλίνδροις, τὸ μὲν πικρὸν καὶ ἀνήμερον τῆς φύσεως ἐνδεικνύμενα, ἐκπληρῶσαι δὲ τὴν μανίαν οὐκ ἔχοντα· οὕτω καὶ τὸ ἐχθρὸν τῆς ἀληθείας γένος οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι στενοχωρούμενοι, πολλὰ, φασὶν, ἐστὶ τὰ πρόσωπα πρὸς οὓς ὁ λόγος γέγονε τοῦ Θεοῦ.
thought_title: The plural 'Let us make man' silences Jewish objections
orientation: Basil is concluding his treatment of the land animals and turning to the creation of humanity, where he will argue that the plural verb in Genesis 1:26 reveals the Father speaking to the Son.
pass_a_gloss: The wild beasts are a demonstration of faith. Have you trusted in the Lord? Upon asp and basilisk you will tread, and you will trample lion and dragon. And you have through faith the authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions. Or do you not see that when Paul was gathering sticks, the viper fastened on him and inflicted no harm, because the holy man was found full of faith? But if you are faithless, fear not so much the wild beast as your own faithlessness, through which you have made yourself easily captured by every corruption. But indeed I perceive that I have long been asked for the things concerning the origin of man, and I almost seem to hear the hearers crying out in their hearts, that we are being taught what sort of things our own things are in nature, but we do not know ourselves. It is necessary therefore to speak, having pushed aside the hesitation that holds us. For truly it seems to be the most difficult of all things to know oneself. For not only does the eye that sees things outside not use seeing upon itself, but also our mind itself, sharply looking down upon the fault of another, is slow toward the recognition of its own defects. For this reason also now the discourse, having sharply gone through the things of others, is sluggish and full of hesitation toward the examination of its own things; and yet it is not more possible to know God from heaven and earth than also from our own constitution, for the one at least who examines himself intelligently; as the prophet says: Your knowledge became wonderful from me; that is, having learned myself thoroughly, I was taught the surpassing character of the wisdom in you. And God said, let us make man. Where is the Jew for me, who, in the things behind, as through certain windows, the light of theology shining through, and a second person being indicated mystically, not yet however clearly manifested, fought against the truth, saying that God was conversing with himself? For he himself said, he says, and he himself made. Let light come to be, and light came to be. There was then also at hand in the things said by them the absurdity. For what blacksmith, or carpenter, or leatherworker, sitting alone at the instruments of his craft, with no one working with him, says to himself, let us make the knife, or let us fit together the plow, or let us finish the sandal; but does he not in silence carry out the activity that falls to him? For it is truly terrible nonsense, that some ruler of himself and overseer sits, urging himself on imperiously and vehemently. But nevertheless those who did not shrink from slandering the Lord himself, what would they not say, having a tongue trained for falsehood? The present voice however completely stops their mouth. And God said, let us make man. Not even now, tell me, is the person solitary? For it is not written, let man come to be, but, Let us make man. As long as the one being taught had not yet appeared, the proclamation of theology was hidden in depth; when now the origin of man is expected, the faith is laid bare, and the doctrine of the truth is shown more clearly. Let us make man. You hear, O fighter against Christ, that he converses with the partner of the creation, through whom also he made the ages, who bears all things by the word of his power. But he does not quietly accept the word of piety; just as the most man-hating of the wild beasts, whenever they are shut up in cages, roar around the bars, showing the bitter and savage character of their nature, but not being able to fulfill their madness; so also the race hostile to the truth, the Jews, being hemmed in, say, Many, they say, are the persons to whom the word of God came.

pass_b_english: The wild beasts are a demonstration of faith. Have you trusted in the Lord? Upon asp and basilisk you will tread, and you will trample lion and dragon (Psalm 90:13 (LXX; Hebrew 91:13)). And you have through faith the authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions (Luke 10:19). Or do you not see that when Paul was gathering sticks, the viper fastened on him and caused him no harm, because the holy man was found to be full of faith (Acts 28:3-5)? But if you are faithless, fear not so much the wild beast as your own faithlessness, through which you have made yourself easy prey to every corruption.

But indeed I sense that I have long been called upon to speak about the creation of man, and I almost seem to hear my hearers crying out in their hearts, 'We are being taught what sort of nature our own things have, but we are ignorant of ourselves.' So I must speak, having pushed aside the hesitation that holds us. For truly it seems to be the most difficult thing of all to know oneself. Not only does the eye, which sees things outside, not use its seeing upon itself, but also our very mind, which sharply discerns another's sin, is slow to recognize its own defects. For this reason even now my discourse, having swiftly gone through things outside us, is sluggish and full of hesitation when it comes to examining our own affairs. And yet it is no more possible to know God from heaven and earth than from our own constitution, at least for the one who examines himself intelligently. As the prophet says, 'Your knowledge became wonderful from me' (Psalm 138:6 (LXX; Hebrew 139:6))—that is, by learning to know myself, I was taught the surpassing greatness of the wisdom in you.

And God said, 'Let us make man' (Genesis 1:26). Where now is the Jew who, in the passages before, when the light of theology was shining through as if through certain windows, and a second Person was being indicated mystically but not yet clearly revealed, fought against the truth, saying that God was conversing with himself? For he himself said, he says, and he himself made. 'Let there be light,' and there was light (Genesis 1:3). Even then, of course, the absurdity in what they said was obvious. For what blacksmith, or carpenter, or leatherworker, sitting alone with the tools of his trade and with no one working with him, says to himself, 'Let us make the knife,' or 'Let us fit together the plow,' or 'Let us finish the sandal'? Does he not rather carry out the work before him in silence? For it is truly terrible nonsense to say that someone sits as ruler and overseer of himself, giving orders to himself in a lordly and urgent manner. But still, those who did not hesitate to slander the Lord himself—what would they not say, having tongues trained for falsehood? The present word, however, completely stops their mouth. 'And God said, Let us make man.' Tell me, is the Person solitary even now? For it is not written, 'Let man be made,' but 'Let us make man.' As long as the one being taught had not yet appeared, the proclamation of theology was hidden in depth. But when the creation of man is now expected, the faith is laid bare, and the doctrine of the truth is shown more clearly. 'Let us make man.' Do you hear, O fighter against Christ, that he is conversing with the partner of his creation, through whom he also made the ages, who upholds all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:2-3)? But he does not quietly accept the word of piety. Just as the most man-hating of wild beasts, when they are shut up in cages, roar around the bars, showing the bitter and savage character of their nature but unable to fulfill their rage, so also the race hostile to the truth, the Jews, being hard pressed, say, 'There are many persons to whom the word of God was addressed.'

last_rejected.quote: Your knowledge became wonderful from me
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἐθαυμαστώθη ἡ γνῶσίς σου ἐξ ἐμοῦ
last_rejected.why: The English reverses the meaning: the Greek says God's knowledge is wonderful 'from me' (i.e., from my perspective/being), not that it 'became wonderful from me' as if the speaker caused it. The Hebrew parallel suggests 'too wonderful for me.' The English 'from me' is ambiguous but 'became wonderful from me' suggests the speaker is the source, which is wrong.
last_rejected.fix: Your knowledge is wonderful beyond me
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξ ἐμοῦ means 'from me'; 'became wonderful from me' is awkward but within range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: the most man-hating of wild beasts
last_rejected.why: μισανθρωπότατα is superlative of μισάνθρωπος, 'man-hating,' but the context compares the Jews to these beasts. The English 'most man-hating of wild beasts' is awkward but correct in sense. However, 'misanthropic' or 'savage toward humans' might be better. Actually this seems within range.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter concedes 'correct in sense'; μισανθρωπότατα as 'most man-hating' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: κοινωνῷ means 'partner' or 'sharer,' but 'partner of his creation' is ambiguous—it could mean 'partner in the act of creating' or 'partner who is a creature.' The Greek τῆς δημιουργίας is objective genitive: 'partner in the work of creation.' 'Co-worker in creation' or 'partner in creation' would be clearer.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Partner of his creation' is within range for κοινωνῷ τῆς δημιουργίας; ambiguity is minor, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: But he does not quietly accept the word of piety
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἀλλ' οὐ γὰρ ἡσυχῇ παραδέχεται τὸν λόγον τῆς εὐσεβείας
last_rejected.why: The subject is unclear in the English. 'He' seems to refer to the Jew/fighter against Christ just mentioned, but the Greek says 'But for he does not quietly accept...' The οὐ γὰρ introduces a new subject—the opponent. The English 'But he does not quietly accept' is ambiguous; it could sound like the Son doesn't accept, or the opponent. The context makes it the opponent, but 'But no—he does not quietly accept' would be clearer.
last_rejected.fix: But no—he does not quietly accept the word of piety
last_rejected.ruling: Context clarifies subject; 'But he does not quietly accept' is within range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: There are many persons to whom the word of God was addressed
last_rejected.source_quote: πολλά, φασίν, ἐστὶ τὰ πρόσωπα πρὸς οὓς ὁ λόγος γέγονε τοῦ Θεοῦ
last_rejected.why: The English misses the point: the Jews are saying 'the word of God was addressed to many persons' as an objection to the 'Let us make' implying only two persons. But 'the word of God was addressed' makes it sound like prophetic address, not 'the word/saying was made/spoken by God to many persons.' More precisely: 'There are many persons to whom God spoke' or 'with whom God conversed.'
last_rejected.fix: There are many persons to whom God spoke
last_rejected.ruling: ὁ λόγος γέγονε τοῦ Θεοῦ = 'word of God was addressed'; rendering is within range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: And God said, 'Let us make man' (Genesis 1:26). Where now is the Jew
last_rejected.source_quote: Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεός, ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον. Ποῦ μοι ὁ Ἰουδαῖος
last_rejected.why: The English omits μοι, 'to me' or 'for my sake'—the rhetorical 'Where is he for me?' or 'Where is the Jew I was speaking of?' This adds a personal, urgent tone. 'Where now is the Jew' loses the μοι.
last_rejected.fix: Where is the Jew I spoke of
last_rejected.ruling: Ποῦ μοι is rhetorical; 'Where now is the Jew' captures the sense; μοι adds tone, not core meaning.
